report.title: Opportunity report

findings.title: Enquiry action only in the footer
findings.observed: On all four service pages, the only enquiry route is a “Contact” link in the footer.
findings.evidence: Page captures of /services/office-interiors and three other service pages. Two competitor studios place an enquiry button beside the service description.
findings.why: A visitor who is ready to ask has to search for the next step, which may add friction at the moment of interest.
findings.action: Add an enquiry action beside each service description, and say what happens after someone enquires.
findings.uncertainty: We can see the layout, not its effect. Analytics access would show how many visitors reach the footer and start an enquiry.

findings.title: AI answers call the studio residential-only
findings.observed: Asked for office interior designers in the studio’s city, the AI assistants we tested described Example Studio as a residential designer.
findings.evidence: Answers recorded from the AI assistants included in the analysis, with the prompts used and the date.
findings.why: If assistants repeat an outdated description, people asking about office projects may not hear about the studio.
findings.action: Make office work explicit on the homepage, service pages and business profiles, and publish office project case studies.
findings.uncertainty: AI answers vary by prompt, time and user. We report what we observed, not a guaranteed ranking.

findings.title: Competitors explain their process; Example Studio doesn’t
findings.observed: Two of three competitor studios describe a typical project timeline and the steps from first call to handover. Example Studio’s pages don’t describe the process.
findings.evidence: Competitor service pages captured on the same day; Example Studio’s service and about pages.
findings.why: Visitors comparing studios may find it easier to picture working with a competitor that explains how a project runs.
findings.action: Add a short “How a project works” section with the typical stages and what the client provides.
findings.uncertainty: Competitor pages show what they claim, not what they deliver. Typical timelines should come from Example Studio’s own projects.

items.a: Your website and the public information around it: the competitors your customers may compare you with, and how you appear in search and AI answers. The report states what was assessed and what wasn’t.

items.q: What do I get in a report?
items.a: Findings in priority order. Each one shows what we observed, the evidence, why it may matter, a recommended action, and any uncertainty or access we’d need to be sure.

items.q: Do I need a report before discussing a project?
items.a: No. If you already know what you need built, tell us about it and we’ll scope it directly.

items.q: Can you see our internal workflows from our website?
items.a: No. A public analysis is an outside-in view. Workflow, sales and operations work starts with a discovery conversation and information you choose to share.
Websites, software, integrations, automation and bespoke AI systems—including assistants and agent teams designed around a specific workflow, with human review where it matters.

items.q: How do you know whether a change worked?
items.a: For implementation projects we agree the measures and the baseline before launch, then review the evidence afterwards. A finished build doesn’t prove an improvement on its own.
